citing_sentences: Figure 1 illustrates the resulting single-axis chunk timeline for semantic counting of person names, where chunks overlapping the annotated name span are accepted and the rest rejected.

abstract: Most speech large language models (SLMs) still process speech in an offline manner — they only start responding after they receive the complete speech segment. However, many real-world applications require streaming speech interaction, for which the audio continuously flows in and the machine is required to answer questions based on the so far received audio chunks. For example, a user may ask the system to continuously count how many times a person’s name has been mentioned while they are speaking. We observe a lack of benchmarks and evaluation protocols for real-time speech interaction. Motivated by this, we propose LibriSpeech-Real-QA, a dataset and a benchmark for real-time speech interaction. We construct different types of real-time question-answer pairs from LibriSpeech to evaluate whether speech LLMs can identify target words in streaming audio. We evaluate several popular real-time commercial models and find that they still tend to respond only after the speech turn has finished. We demonstrate that we can enable a pretrained SLM to perform this task, where we explore several modeling designs and establish a solid baseline for future research.

sections.body: The paper argues that speech models should answer while audio is still arriving, as people do in conversation. It notes that full-duplex evaluations cover turn-taking, interruptions and backchannels, but not fine-grained streaming behavior. The authors build LibriSpeech-Real-QA from LibriSpeech with four task types that cross lexical or semantic targets with detection or counting. They score emission-level recall, precision, F1-score and onset delay, and they finetune Qwen2.5-Omni as a baseline.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing speech models respond only after a full turn, so the paper introduces LibriSpeech-Real-QA, a benchmark for event-triggered streaming interaction.

sections.body: Each utterance is annotated with word timestamps from forced alignment, with 20 semantic categories assigned by an LLM, and with negative samples where the target is absent. A sample is kept only when repeated occurrences of a target are more than one second apart. An emission counts as a hit when its onset falls inside the event's acceptance window, which runs from word start to word end plus a grace period g, and when its content matches the event and the prompt. Table 1 lists sample counts for train, dev and benchmark splits.
sections.heading: Benchmark Design
sections.headline: Four tasks ask models to emit target words or running counts at the moment they are heard, scored on both content and onset time.

sections.body: Audio is split into chunks of C seconds, and at each chunk boundary the model either emits the target content or a silence token. Each user turn holds only the newly arrived chunk, so every decision sees only the causal prefix. The loss averages speak and silence decisions separately, because silent chunks would otherwise dominate training. The audio encoder is frozen, LoRA adapters with rank r=16 are applied to the thinker attention and FFN projections, and special tokens stay trainable. Training uses a learning rate of 1.5×10^-4 and batch size 96.
sections.heading: Streaming Model Baseline
sections.headline: Qwen2.5-Omni-7B is finetuned to speak or stay silent at each fixed-length audio chunk, using a rebalanced loss.

sections.body: Four real-time services are compared with pretrained and offline-finetuned Qwen2.5-Omni-7B and with the streaming model at 400, 280 and 160 ms chunk durations. The streaming model reaches 0.988/0.968 F1 on lexical detection at +1c with 400 ms chunks. The text reports that the services' mean onset delays are several seconds, consistent with responding near the end of an utterance. Offline inference remains stronger on both counting tasks, but it is a post-audio reference and not directly comparable. Removing negative samples gives the lowest F1 on all four tasks.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: The finetuned streaming model outscores the evaluated real-time services on all four tasks, while offline inference stays stronger on counting.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes the benchmark and its protocol, which scores both the content and the timing of model responses. It states that existing real-time speech APIs often respond near the end of an utterance rather than when a queried event occurs. It reports that streaming finetuning yields causal, event-level responses and baselines across chunk durations. The authors describe the accuracy-delay trade-offs as task-dependent. They state that the benchmark provides a basis for models that answer while speech is still unfolding.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Real-time services tend to respond near utterance end, while finetuning gives a causal baseline with chunk-dependent accuracy-delay trade-offs.
